title: The poor
hookLine: not a project, but people with names
tomorrow: Nia asks Grace what she actually believes. what does she say?

lines: THE POOR MAN HAS A NAME.
cards: A fundraising video shows a face but never a name. A report counts the meals served. Useful, and still a little strange: people turn into totals.
In one of Jesus' stories it runs the other way. The rich man has a closet full of purple and no name at all. The poor man lying at his gate has one: Lazarus.

teach.b: Luke tells it this way: “There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day: And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores.”
The story doesn't make the rich man cruel.
He doesn't beat Lazarus or drive him off. He feasts, with a man lying at his gate, and the story never shows him noticing.

Later, the tables turn: it is the rich man who asks for Lazarus, by name, to bring him a drop of water. Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: in Luke's telling, the poor man gets a name and the rich man doesn't.
Proverbs puts the stakes high: “He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again.”

And James warns against kind words with nothing behind them: telling someone hungry, “Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled,” and not giving the things the body needs. Giving, meals and shelters all matter.
Today's line is narrower than any of that: not a project. A project has totals and outcomes. A person has a name, a story, and a face you'd know again.

how: Christians serve the poor through giving, food pantries, shelters and meals, and some churches also encourage simply getting to know people by name, sharing a table rather than only handing something across it.

o: people in need, each with a name and a story
people who chose to live simply for religious reasons
people who don't give enough to the church

games.q: your church's food drive posts, "we served 200 people!" a friend says the post feels off. what would Luke 16 add?
o: counting is wrong; never post numbers.
the numbers matter, but each one is a person with a name.
the post is fine; the poor are a cause, not individuals.
games.why: giving and counting both have a place. Luke's story just names the poor man and leaves the rich man nameless: not a project, a person.

practice: Take a coin or a bill from a pocket or wallet, or just picture one, and look at it closely. Then let a face come to mind: someone you pass who has less.
If you know their name, say it quietly; if you don't yet, let that be the thing you'd like to learn.

wordCard.voice: The poor. Not a category or a cause, but people with names, at the gates we pass every day.

orig.note: Greek: poor; the word Luke uses for Lazarus in 16:20 (beggar in the KJV).

carryVoice: Your line: not a project. A person, with a name. Seven lines, a week of people, done.
